¶
'''bestraddle''' (bẹ̄-strad′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''straddle.''] To bestride. See ''straddle.''

'''bestraught†''' (bẹ̄-strât′), ''pp.'' [A modification of ''distraught'', with prefix ''be-'' for ''dis-'': see ''distraught.''] Distracted; mad: as, “I am not ''bestraught,''” ''Shak.'', T. of the S., Ind., ii.

'''bestraughted†''' (bẹ̄-strâ′ted), ''a.'' [Irreg. < ''bestraught.''] Distracted. ''Norden.'' [Rare.]

'''bestraw†''' (bẹ̄-strâ′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''straw'' for ''strew.''] An obsolete form of ''bestrew.''

'''bestreak''' (bẹ̄-strēk′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''streak.''] To mark or cover with streaks.

'''bestrew, bestrow''' (bẹ̄-strö′, -strō′), ''v. t.''; pret. ''bestrewed'', ''bestrowed'', pp. ''bestrewed'', ''bestrewn'', ''bestrowed'', ''bestrown'', ppr. ''bestrewing'', ''bestrowing.'' [< ME. ''bistrewen'', < AS. ''bestreówian'' (= D. ''bestrooijen'' = MHG. ''beströuwen'', G. ''bestreuen'' = Sw. ''beströ'' = Dan. ''beströ''), < ''be-'' + ''streówian'', strew: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''strew'', ''strow''.] '''1.''' To strew or scatter about; throw or drop here and there.
{{smaller block|<poem>Those blossoms also, and those dropping gums,
That lie ''bestrown.''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 631.}}}}
'''2.''' To strew anything upon; cover or partially cover with things strewn or scattered.
{{smaller block|<poem>Discord shall ''bestrew''
The union of your bed with weeds so loathly,
That you shall hate it both.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1.}}
<poem>Strip the bough whose mellow fruit ''bestrews''
The ripening corn beneath it.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Between Namur and Liege.}}}}

'''bestrid''' (bẹ̄-strid′). Preterit and past participle of ''bestride.''
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''bestride''' (bē-strīd′), ''v. t.''; pret. ''bestrode'' or ''bestrid'', pp. ''bestridden'', ''bestrid'', improperly ''bestrided''† (Sterne), ppr. ''bestriding''. [< ME. ''bestriden'' (pret. ''bestrood'', ''bestrode'', pp. wanting), < AS. ''bestrīdan'' (''hors bestrīdan''—Lye), < ''be-'' + ''strīdan'', stride.] '''1.''' To straddle over; mount astride of; stretch the legs or corresponding parts across so as to embrace: as, to ''bestride'' a horse; spectacles ''bestriding'' the nose.
{{smaller block|<poem>Why, man, he doth ''bestride'' the narrow world
Like a Colossus.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., i. 2.}}
The animal he ''bestrode'' was a broken-down plough-horse.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 436.}}}}
'''2.''' To step over; cross by stepping.
{{smaller block|<poem>When I first my wedded mistress saw
''Bestride'' my threshold.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iv. 5.}}}}

'''bestrode''' (bē-strōd′). Preterit of ''bestride''.

'''bestrow''', ''v. t.'' See ''bestrew''.

'''bestrut†''' (bē-strut′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''strut.''] To distend.
{{smaller block|Her paps ''bestrut'' with milk.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 519.}}}}

'''bestuck''' (bē-stuk′). Preterit and past participle of ''bestick''.

'''bestud''' (bē-stud′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bestudded'', ppr. ''bestudding''. [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stud''<sup>2</sup>.] To set with or as with studs; adorn with bosses.
{{smaller block|<poem>The unsought diamonds
Would so imblaze the forehead of the deep,
And so ''bestud'' with stars, that they below
Would grow inured to light.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 734.}}}}

'''beswaddle''' (bē-swod′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''swaddle.''] To envelop in swaddling-clothes. ''W. Whitehead.''

''Gower.''

'''beswinge†''' (bē-swinj′), ''v. t.'' [ME. not found; AS. ''beswingan'', only in pp. ''beswungen'', scourge, beat, < ''be-'' + ''swingan'', scourge, swinge.] To scourge; beat.
{{smaller block|You had best to use your sword better, lest I ''beswinge'' you.
{{right|''Greene'', Orlando Furioso.}}}}

'''beswink†''', ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''beswinken'', < AS. ''beswincan'', earn by toil, < ''be-'' + ''swincan'', swink, toil: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''swink''.] To earn.
{{smaller block|<poem>That of a poison which they drunke
They hadden that they have ''beswunke.''</poem>
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., i. 131.}}}}

'''besy†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''busy''.

'''bet<sup>1</sup>†''' (bet), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''bet'', < AS. ''bet'' = OFries. ''bet'' = OS. ''bat'', ''bet'' = OD. ''bat'', ''bet'' = OHG. MHG. ''baz'', G. ''bass'' = Icel. ''betr'' = Goth. *''batis'' (in adj. ''batiza''), better, orig. adj. in the neut. acc. with reg. compar. suffix (lost in AS., etc.; hence the later form ''betere'', ''betre'', E. ''batten''<sup>1</sup>, become or make better, improve, AS. ''bōt'', E. ''boot''<sup>1</sup>, advantage, improvement, AS. ''bētan'', E. ''beet''<sup>2</sup>, improve, etc.: see ''batten''<sup>1</sup>, ''battle''<sup>3</sup>, ''boot''<sup>1</sup>, ''beet''<sup>2</sup>, etc.] Obsolete and earlier Middle English form of ''better''<sup>1</sup>.

to another who pledges a forfeit in return on the opposite contingency.—'''2.''' That which is wagered; also, that about which a wager is made.

{{smaller block|But, on: Six Barbary horses against six French swords, their assigns, and three liberal conceited carriages: that’s the French ''bet'' against the Danish.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 2.}}}}

'''bet<sup>3</sup>†.''' An obsolete preterit of ''beat''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Beta<sup>1</sup>''' (bē′tä̤), ''n.'' [L., a beet: see ''beet''<sup>1</sup>.] A genus of apetalous plants, natural order ''Chenopodiaceæ''. See ''beet''<sup>1</sup>.

'''beta<sup>2</sup>''' (bē′tä̤), ''n.'' [L., repr. Gr. βῆτα, name of the character Β, β.] '''1.''' The second letter of the Greek alphabet, corresponding to English ''B'' or ''b''.—'''2.''' As a classifier in astronomy, chemistry, etc., the second in any series. See ''alpha'', 3.

'''betacism''' (bē′tạ-sizm), ''n.'' [< NL. ''betacismus'', < L. ''beta'', the (Greek) letter β, ''b''. Cf. ''iotacism'', ''rhotacism''.] Conversion of other sounds to, or their confusion with, a ''b''-sound.

{{smaller block|Even these forms were threatened with destruction by the spread of ''Betacismus'', whereby amavit was pronounced like amabit, and vice versa.
{{right|''Amer. Jour. Philol.'', VI. 501.}}}}

'''betag''' (bẹ̄-tag′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''betagged'', ppr. ''betagging''. [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tag''.] To furnish with a tag; deck with tags.

{{smaller block|''Betagged'' with verse.
{{right|''Churchill'', The Ghost, iv.}}}}

'''betail''' (bẹ̄-tāl′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tail''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To furnish with a tail: as, “''betailed'' and bepowdered,” ''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, iii.—
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''2.''' To take the tail off: a word jocularly formed on the analogy of ''behead.''

{{smaller block|[The sportsman] puts his heavy boot on the beast’s body, and there both beheads and ''betails'' him. {{right|''Trollope.''}}}}

'''betain''' (bē′tạ-in), ''n.'' [Irreg. < L. ''beta'' + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.] A chemical base found in the common beet and mangel-wurzel.

'''betake'''<sup>1</sup> (bē-tāk′), ''v.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''take.'' The corresponding ME. form ''betaken, bitaken'' (pret. ''betok,'' pp. ''betaken'') seems to have been used only in the senses of ''betake''<sup>2</sup> or ''beteach,'' with which it was confused. There is no AS. *''betacan''; but cf. Sw. ''betaka'' = Dan. ''betage,'' take, deprive, cut off.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To seize; take hold of; take.

{{smaller block|Then to his handes that writt he did ''betake.''
{{right|''Spenser,'' F. Q., I. xii. 25.}}}}

'''2.''' Reflexively, to take one’s self (to); repair; resort; have recourse.

{{smaller block|<poem>The rest, in imitation, to like arms
''Betook them.'' ''Milton,'' P. L., vi. 663.</poem>
''Betake you'' to your silence, and your sleep.
{{right|''B. Jonson,'' Volpone, i. 1.}}
They ''betook themselves'' to treaty and submission.
{{right|''Burke,'' Abridg. of Eng. Hist., i. 1.}}}}

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To take one’s self.

{{smaller block|But here ly downe, and to thy rest ''betake.''
{{right|''Spenser,'' F. Q., I. ix. 44.}}}}

'''betake'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''v. t.''; pret. ''betook, betaught,'' pp. ''betaught,'' ppr. ''betaking.'' [ME. ''betaken,'' etc., with forms prop. belonging to ''betake''<sup>1</sup>, q. v., but with various senses of ''betæcen, betechen,'' beteach: see

''beteach.''] Same as ''beteach.''

'''betalk†''' (bē-tâk′), ''v. i.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''talk.''] To talk repeatedly. ''Drayton.''

'''betallow''' (bē-tal′ō), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tallow.''] To cover with tallow. ''Ford.''

'''betaught†''' (bē-tât′). Preterit of ''betake''<sup>2</sup> and ''beteach.''

'''bete<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v.'', '''bete<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'', '''bete<sup>3</sup>†''', ''v.'', etc. Obsolete form of ''beat''<sup>1</sup>, ''beet''<sup>1</sup>, ''beet''<sup>2</sup>, etc.

'''bête''' (bāt), ''n.'' [F., < OF. ''beste'', a beast: see ''beast.''] In the game of solo, a forfeit.—{{smaller|'''Bête noire''' (F. pron. bāt nwor). [F., literally black beast.] A bugbear; a person or thing regarded with special dislike or aversion.}}
{{smaller block|The newspapers have some words of this sort dear to them, but the ''bêtes noires'' of all lovers of straightforward English, such as “peruse” and “replete.”
{{right|''The Atlantic'', LVII. 425.}}}}

'''beteach†''' (bē-tēch′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''betechen'', ''bitechen'', ''betæcen'' (pret. ''betauhte'', ''betahte'', pp. ''betauht'', ''betaht''), < AS. ''betǣcan'' (pret. ''betǣhte'', pp. ''betǣht''), show, assign, give over, deliver, commit, < ''be-'' + ''tǣcan'', show, teach: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''teach.'' Owing to a similarity of form, the ME. ''betaken'' (pret. ''betook'', ''betok'', pp. ''betaken''), < ''be-'' + ''taken'', take (see ''betake''<sup>1</sup>), was confused with ''betechen'', and used in the same senses.] '''1.''' To give; hand over; deliver up.
{{smaller block|Judas Iscariot wente forth to the princis of prestis, and said to hem, What wolen ye give to me and I schal ''bitake'' him to you?
{{right|''Wyclif'', Mat. xxvi. 14, 15.}}}}
'''2.''' To intrust; commit; recommend to the care of.
{{smaller block|<poem>Such a rym the devel I ''byteche.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Tale of Melibeus, l. 6.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bestorm|535|beteach}}</noinclude>storm, agitate.] To overtake with a storm; assail with storms: as, “boats ''bestormed,''” ''Sir W. Davenant,'' Gondibert, iii. 6.
{{smaller block|<poem>All is sea besides,
Sinks under us, ''bestorms,'' and then devours.</poem>
{{right|''Young,'' Night Thoughts, iv.}}}}

'''bestow''' (bē-stō′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bestowen, bistowen''; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''stow'', place: see ''stow''.]   '''1.''' To lay up in store; deposit for safe keeping; stow; place.
{{smaller block|I have no room where to ''bestow'' my fruits. {{right|Luke xii. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|He ''bestowed'' it in a pouch lined with perfumed leather.
{{right|''Scott.''}}}}
{{smaller block|To all appearance I must be [engaged] for many months to come in turning out, examining, sorting, and ''bestowing'' these materials.
{{right|''Dr. J. A. H. Murray,'' 8th Ann. Add. to Philol. Soc.}}}}
'''2.''' To lodge, or find quarters for; provide with accommodation.
{{smaller block|Well, my masters, I’ll leave him with you; now I see him ''bestowed,'' I’ll go look for my goods.
{{right|''B. Jonson,'' Bartholomew Fair, iv. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' To dispose of.
{{smaller block|Give me but the name and nature of your malefactor, and I’ll ''bestow'' him according to his merits.
{{right|''Middleton (and others),'' The Widow, i. 1.}}}}
'''4.''' To give; confer; impart gratuitously: followed by ''on'' or ''upon'' before the recipient: as, to ''bestow'' praise or blame impartially.
{{smaller block|Consecrate yourselves . . . to the Lord, . . . that he may ''bestow upon'' you a blessing. {{right|Ex. xxxii. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|Though I ''bestow'' all my goods to feed the poor . . . and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing. {{right|1 Cor. xiii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Around its entry nodding poppies grow,
And all cool simples that sweet rest ''bestow.''</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Ceyx and Alcyone, l. 287.}}}}
{{smaller block|Did you ''bestow'' your fortune, or did you only lend it?
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, lxvi.}}}}
'''5.''' To give in marriage.
{{smaller block|I could have ''bestowed'' her upon a fine gentleman.
{{right|''Tatler.''}}}}
'''6.''' To apply; make use of; use; employ.
{{smaller block|<poem>I determine to ''bestow''
Some time in learning languages abroad.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Love’s Sacrifice, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Otherwise the whole force of the war would have been infallibly ''bestowed'' there. {{right|''Swift.''}}}}
'''7†.''' To behave or deport.
{{smaller block|<poem>The boy . . . ''bestows'' himself
Like a ripe sister. ''Shak.'', As you Like it, iv. 3.</poem>}}
='''Syn. 4.''' ''Confer'', ''Grant'', etc. See ''give.''

'''bestowable''' (bē-stō′a-bl), ''a.''   [< ''bestow'' + ''-able.'']   Capable of being bestowed.

'''bestowal''' (bẹ̄-stō′ạl), ''n.''   [< ''bestow'' + ''-al.'']   Bestowment.

{{smaller block|It had been ''bet'' for me still to have kept my quiet chair.

'''bet'''<sup>2</sup> (bet), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''bet'' or ''betted'', ppr. ''betting''.   [First in early mod. E.; prob. short for ''abet'' (cf. ''bate''<sup>2</sup>, short for ''abate''); if so, prob. first as a noun, instigation, encouragement, support, backing, whence the verb, to give support, etc.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To pledge as a forfeit to another who makes a similar pledge in return, on a future contingency, in support of an affirmation or opinion; stake; wager.
{{smaller block|John of Gaunt loved him well, and ''betted'' much money on his head.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iii. 2.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To lay a wager; stake money or anything of value upon a contingency.—'''You bet''', {{smaller|certainly; of course. [U. S., originally California, slang.]}}
{{smaller block|<poem>“Friend,” said I to a Jehu, whose breath suggested gin,
“Can thee convey me straightway to a reputable inn?”
His answer’s gross irrelevance I shall not soon forget—
Instead of simply yea or nay, he gruffly said, “''You bet!''”</poem>
{{right|''The Century'', XI. 142.}}}}

'''bet'''<sup>2</sup> (bet), ''n.''   [See the verb.]   '''1.''' The pledging of some valuable thing, as money (or of the doing of some onerous act), to be forfeited, in case some future event happens contrary to the assertion or belief of the one making the pledge, to another who pledges a forfeit in return on the opposite contingency.—'''2.''' That which is wagered; also, that about which a wager is made.

{{smaller block|But, on: Six Barbary horses against six French swords, their assigns, and three liberal conceited carriages: that’s the French ''bet'' against the Danish.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 2.}}}}

'''bet<sup>3</sup>†.''' An obsolete preterit of ''beat''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Beta<sup>1</sup>''' (bē′tä̤), ''n.''   [L., a beet: see ''beet''<sup>1</sup>.]   A genus of apetalous plants, natural order ''Chenopodiaceæ''. See ''beet''<sup>1</sup>.

'''beta<sup>2</sup>''' (bē′tä̤), ''n.''   [L., repr. Gr. βῆτα, name of the character Β, β.]   '''1.''' The second letter of the Greek alphabet, corresponding to English ''B'' or ''b''.—'''2.''' As a classifier in astronomy, chemistry, etc., the second in any series. See ''alpha'', 3.

'''betacism''' (bē′tạ-sizm), ''n.''   [< NL. ''betacismus'', < L. ''beta'', the (Greek) letter β, ''b''. Cf. ''iotacism'', ''rhotacism''.]   Conversion of other sounds to, or their confusion with, a ''b''-sound.

{{smaller block|Even these forms were threatened with destruction by the spread of ''Betacismus'', whereby amavit was pronounced like amabit, and vice versa.
{{right|''Amer. Jour. Philol.'', VI. 501.}}}}

'''betag''' (bẹ̄-tag′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''betagged'', ppr. ''betagging''.   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tag''.]   To furnish with a tag; deck with tags.

{{smaller block|''Betagged'' with verse.
{{right|''Churchill'', The Ghost, iv.}}}}

'''betail''' (bẹ̄-tāl′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tail''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' To furnish with a tail: as, “''betailed'' and bepowdered,” ''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, iii.—

'''2.''' To take the tail off: a word jocularly formed on the analogy of ''behead.''

{{smaller block|[The sportsman] puts his heavy boot on the beast’s body, and there both beheads and ''betails'' him. {{right|''Trollope.''}}}}

'''betain''' (bē′tạ-in), ''n.''   [Irreg. < L. ''beta'' + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]   A chemical base found in the common beet and mangel-wurzel.

'''betake'''<sup>1</sup> (bē-tāk′), ''v.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''take.'' The corresponding ME. form ''betaken, bitaken'' (pret. ''betok,'' pp. ''betaken'') seems to have been used only in the senses of ''betake''<sup>2</sup> or ''beteach,'' with which it was confused. There is no AS. *''betacan''; but cf. Sw. ''betaka'' = Dan. ''betage,'' take, deprive, cut off.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To seize; take hold of; take.

{{smaller block|Then to his handes that writt he did ''betake.''
{{right|''Spenser,'' F. Q., I. xii. 25.}}}}

'''2.''' Reflexively, to take one’s self (to); repair; resort; have recourse.

<poem>The rest, in imitation, to like arms
''Betook them.''   ''Milton,'' P. L., vi. 663.</poem>
{{smaller block|''Betake you'' to your silence, and your sleep.
{{right|''B. Jonson,'' Volpone, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|They ''betook themselves'' to treaty and submission.
{{right|''Burke,'' Abridg. of Eng. Hist., i. 1.}}}}

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To take one’s self.

{{smaller block|But here ly downe, and to thy rest ''betake.''
{{right|''Spenser,'' F. Q., I. ix. 44.}}}}

'''betake'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''v. t.''; pret. ''betook, betaught,'' pp. ''betaught,'' ppr. ''betaking.''   [ME. ''betaken,'' etc., with forms prop. belonging to ''betake''<sup>1</sup>, q. v., but with various senses of ''betæcen, betechen,'' beteach: see ''beteach.'']   Same as ''beteach.''

'''betalk†''' (bē-tâk′), ''v. i.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''talk.'']   To talk repeatedly.   ''Drayton.''

'''betallow''' (bē-tal′ō), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tallow.'']   To cover with tallow.   ''Ford.''

'''betaught†''' (bē-tât′). Preterit of ''betake''<sup>2</sup> and ''beteach.''

'''bete<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v.'', '''bete<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'', '''bete<sup>3</sup>†''', ''v.'', etc. Obsolete form of ''beat''<sup>1</sup>, ''beet''<sup>1</sup>, ''beet''<sup>2</sup>, etc.

'''bête''' (bāt), ''n.''   [F., < OF. ''beste'', a beast: see ''beast.'']   In the game of solo, a forfeit.—{{smaller|'''Bête noire''' (F. pron. bāt nwor). [F., literally black beast.] A bugbear; a person or thing regarded with special dislike or aversion.}}
{{smaller block|The newspapers have some words of this sort dear to them, but the ''bêtes noires'' of all lovers of straightforward English, such as “peruse” and “replete.”
{{right|''The Atlantic'', LVII. 425.}}}}

'''beteach†''' (bē-tēch′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''betechen'', ''bitechen'', ''betæcen'' (pret. ''betauhte'', ''betahte'', pp. ''betauht'', ''betaht''), < AS. ''betǣcan'' (pret. ''betǣhte'', pp. ''betǣht''), show, assign, give over, deliver, commit, < ''be-'' + ''tǣcan'', show, teach: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''teach.'' Owing to a similarity of form, the ME. ''betaken'' (pret. ''betook'', ''betok'', pp. ''betaken''), < ''be-'' + ''taken'', take (see ''betake''<sup>1</sup>), was confused with ''betechen'', and used in the same senses.]   '''1.''' To give; hand over; deliver up.
{{smaller block|Judas Iscariot wente forth to the princis of prestis, and said to hem, What wolen ye give to me and I schal ''bitake'' him to you?
{{right|''Wyclif'', Mat. xxvi. 14, 15.}}}}
'''2.''' To intrust; commit; recommend to the care of.
{{smaller block|<poem>Such a rym the devel I ''byteche.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Tale of Melibeus, l. 6.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
